es.q: Define the components of a portal triad and list two essential functions of bile within the gastrointestinal system.
es.m: A portal triad consists of a bile duct, a hepatic artery branch, and a portal vein branch (2 marks). The two essential functions of bile are: 1. Elimination of water-insoluble bilirubin, excess cholesterol, and xenobiotics. 2. Emulsification of dietary fat in the gut. (3 marks)

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Gastrointestinal pathology includes inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic and vascular diseases that alter gut structure and function. Clinicians must link symptoms, risk factors and investigations to reach a precise diagnosis and guide treatment.

sections.p: Gastrointestinal pathology refers to any disease process that damages the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis or serosa of the GI tract, diagnosed by history, exam and targeted investigations.
b: Diagnosis integrates symptom pattern, risk factors and objective findings.

t.b: What structural lesion is present and does histology confirm inflammation, infection or neoplasia? Positive result directs specific therapy.
Is an infectious organism present? Detects parasites, bacteria, viruses; guides antimicrobial choice.
Do markers suggest malignancy? Elevated levels support cancer work‑up but are not diagnostic alone.

sections.p: Severity is staged by established systems: e.g., Crohn’s disease (Montreal classification), ulcerative colitis (Mayo score), and colorectal cancer (TNM). Staging guides prognosis and therapy intensity.
b: Higher stage = greater risk of complications and need for aggressive treatment.

t.b: What is tumor size, nodal involvement, metastasis? Determines cancer stage and surgical candidacy.
How extensive is colonic inflammation? Scores 0‑3; higher scores need systemic therapy.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by inflammation, infection, vascular injury and neoplasia. In low‑resource settings, infections and HIV‑related disease are common.
b: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis)
Helicobacter pylori infection
Amoebic colitis (Entamoeba histolytica)
Tuberculous enteritis (especially in HIV)
Ischemic colitis (hypotension, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion)
Colorectal adenocarcinoma

sections.p: Patients may have abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, weight loss, bleeding or systemic signs like fever. Pattern of pain (periumbilical vs. left lower quadrant) helps narrow the differential.
b: Chronic diarrhea with weight loss → IBD or infection
Upper abdominal pain relieved by food → peptic ulcer disease
Bright red rectal bleeding → hemorrhoids, ulcerative colitis, cancer

sections.p: Select tests that answer the clinical question; when a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative.

t.b: Is there anemia or leukocytosis? Low hemoglobin suggests chronic bleeding; high WBC points to infection or inflammation.
Is there hidden GI bleeding? Positive result prompts endoscopic evaluation.
Are there masses, thickened bowel loops, or free fluid? Detects hepatobiliary disease and large lesions.

sections.p: Identify features that signal imminent danger or irreversible damage.
b: Acute massive GI bleed → hemodynamic collapse
Perforation with peritonitis → sepsis
Obstruction with vomiting and distension → bowel ischemia
Progressive weight loss >10% → possible malignancy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor for complications.
b: H. pylori eradication: clarithromycin‑based triple therapy (chosen for high cure rates; avoid metronidazole if resistance high).
IBD flares: systemic corticosteroids to induce remission; azathioprine or biologics for maintenance (avoid long‑term steroids due to toxicity).
Ischemic colitis: restore perfusion, bowel rest, broad‑spectrum antibiotics if necrosis suspected.
Colorectal cancer: surgical resection ± adjuvant chemotherapy (avoid monotherapy with agents that cause severe neuropathy in malnourished patients).

sections.p: Regular surveillance prevents progression and detects early recurrence.
b: Colonoscopy every 3–5 years after polyp removal or for IBD surveillance.
H. pylori test‑of‑cure after therapy.
Vaccination against hepatitis B and rotavirus in endemic areas.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic GI pathology must be distinguished to avoid mismanagement.
b: Irritable bowel syndrome vs. ulcerative colitis (IBS lacks inflammation on labs/endoscopy).
Gastric ulcer vs. gastric cancer (cancer shows irregular margins, deeper invasion).
Diverticulitis vs. appendicitis (location of pain and CT findings differ).

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal, especially in early disease or resource‑limited settings.
b: Fecal occult blood can be negative in right‑sided colon cancer.
Serum CEA may be normal in early colorectal cancer.
Stool microscopy may miss low‑level parasites; PCR is more sensitive.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with rigidity
Persistent rectal bleeding with dizziness or fainting

faq.q: Why is endoscopy preferred over imaging for ulcer diagnosis?
faq.a: It visualizes the mucosa directly and allows biopsy, giving definitive histology.
No, but remission can be achieved with medication and surgery when needed.

faq.q: What is the role of H. pylori testing after treatment?
faq.a: To confirm eradication and prevent recurrence of ulcer disease.
